inherit.why: The parent's wrapped-thumb rule (Baechle and Earle, thumbs around the bar) carries over to a dumbbell handle by reasoning (MECH); this card adds no separate thumb source.
Same hold archetype and a hanging load as the parent, so the neutral wrist range applies (MECH).

claims.text: Balance on one leg and hold the dumbbell in the opposite hand; the standing knee stays slightly bent and the back straight.

quotes.text: Balance on the left leg while holding a dumbbell in the right hand. Keep the left knee slightly bent and the back straight while leaning forward on the left hip

claims.text: While leaning forward, straighten the free leg and point its toes to help balance.

quotes.text: (tip: while leaning forward straighten the right leg and point the right toes to help stay balanced.)

claims.text: Keep the arm straight so the dumbbell lowers directly in front of the standing leg.

quotes.text: Keep the arm straight so the dumbbell is lowering directly in front of the left leg.

claims.text: To stand, push the standing foot into the floor and lower the free leg; pause balanced before the next rep.

quotes.text: Push the left foot into the floor, pull back on the left knee, and lower the right leg to stand up, keeping the grip on the dumbbell. Pause in a balanced position before performing the next repetition.

claims.text: Keep the hips still; the side of the lifted leg should not rotate upwards.

quotes.text: Make sure to keep your hips still; you don’t want the side with your lifted leg to start rotating upwards.
quotes.where: How to Do Single Leg Romanian Deadlifts

claims.text: If balance is hard, keep the toes of the lifted leg touching the floor.

quotes.text: If you have trouble keeping your balance, you can keep the toes of your lifted leg touching the floor to add some stability.

claims.text: Faults to avoid include rounding the back and shoulders, not keeping the neck neutral, and lowering the dumbbell too low; many trainees try to touch the dumbbell to the floor, which rounds the back.

quotes.text: rounding the back and shoulders, not packing the neck, lowering the DB too low, to name a few
many trainees make the mistake of trying to touch the DB all the way to the floor, resulting in a significant amount of flexion

claims.text: Keep the whole back side in a straight line from head to toes, with the neck neutral.

quotes.text: Many will view this as looking down, but in fact, you’re just keeping the neck in a neutral position.
you want to think of your entire backside as making a straight line (said differently, arch your back) from your head all the way down to your toes.

claims.text: Think 'hips back' rather than reaching the dumbbell down; stop at about mid-shin, where the hamstrings feel strong tension.

quotes.text: So, instead of actively thinking about lowering the DB, all you need to do is think “hips back,” until the DB reaches roughly mid-shin level.
At that point, you shoulde feel some pretty significant tension in the hamstrings.

claims.text: Keep a soft standing knee, about 15-20 degrees bent, not locked.

quotes.text: It shouldn’t be locked or stiff.  Ideally, you want about 15-20 degrees of knee flexion.

claims.text: Drive the free leg's heel toward the ceiling; weight shifts back into the standing heel, not the toes.

quotes.text: Likewise, as you push back, you should feel the brunt of your weight shift back into your supporting leg’s heel.
grip the DB HARD, push your hips back, and think about driving your moving leg’s heel up towards the ceiling.

claims.text: Working in a shorter, usable range is fine while hip control builds.

quotes.text: So, if you have to limit the ROM due to poor hip stablity (for instance), that’s fine.

claims.text: Single-leg RDLs are among the most advanced single-leg movements, even for experienced lifters.

quotes.text: The fact of the matter is, even for trainees with a fair amount of experience under the bar, 1-Legged RDLs are about as advanced as they get as far as single leg movements go.

claims.text: In trained men, the dumbbell single-leg RDL produced very high glute and hamstring (biceps femoris) activity; holding the load on the opposite side raised glute and back activity (flywheel), with no dumbbell-vs-flywheel difference.

quotes.text: The overall results demonstrated a very high level of SGM (105.4%-168.6%) and BF (69.6%-122.4%) muscle activities.
Strength coaches may adopt dumbbell or flywheel SLRDL exercises using the contralateral loading position to simultaneously strengthen the hip extensors and trunk stabilizers effectively.

claims.text: The lower-back muscles (erector spinae) work in the single-leg RDL, more so when the load is held on the opposite side (flywheel data).

quotes.text: A significant moderate increase of sEMG signals in GM, IGM, and ES (dominant side) and a large increase in SGM activity during concentric action when the loading position of flywheel SLRDL was changed from ipsilateral to the contralateral side.

claims.text: Tempo: about 1-2 s up and 1-2 s down, then a balanced pause at the top.

quotes.text: using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC).
Pause in a balanced position before performing the next repetition.

claims.text: Add load in small steps (2-10%) only once the target reps are exceeded by one or two.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: Grip the dumbbell hard; do not think of it as lowering the dumbbell with the arm.

quotes.text: This is important because you can’t think of this movement as actively lowering the DB with your arm
CRUSH the dumbbell with your grip.

claims.text: Finish all reps on one side, then switch legs.

quotes.text: Finish all your reps on one side first, and then repeat on the other leg.
quotes.where: How to Do Single Leg Romanian Deadlifts

claims.text: Back pain with weakness or numbness in both legs, or loss of feeling around the genitals, needs 999; pain not better after a few weeks needs a GP.

quotes.text: Call 999 or go to A&E if:
pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs
a loss of feeling around your genitals or anus
See a GP if:
it does not improve after treating it at home for a few weeks

plate.viewWhy: The hinge, the free leg in line with the back and the dumbbell in front of the standing leg are front-to-back positions (c3, c8); the hip opening fault is a rotation (c5) and cannot be drawn in any view.
plate.equipment: One dumbbell in the hand opposite the standing leg (c1), floor line. Bodyweight version: same body, no dumbbell.
plate.start: Standing on one leg, standing knee soft at about 15-20 degrees (c10), dumbbell hanging from a straight arm (c3), free foot just off the floor.
plate.end: Hips pushed back, trunk and free leg forming one straight line from head to heel (c8, c2), standing knee still soft (c10), dumbbell at about mid-shin in front of the standing leg (c9, c3).

checkpoints.label: Straight line
checkpoints.what: Head, back and free leg in one line, neck neutral.

checkpoints.label: Soft knee
checkpoints.what: Standing knee bent about 15-20 degrees, not locked.

checkpoints.label: Mid-shin
checkpoints.what: Dumbbell stops about mid-shin, in front of the standing leg.

mistake.what: Back and shoulders round as the dumbbell is reached toward the floor.
mistake.why: The hip of the lifted leg rotating up (c5) is a rotation the engine cannot draw; rounding while reaching the dumbbell too low is drawable side-on, and Gentilcore says many trainees do it (c7).
mistake.rankNote: No source ranks single-leg RDL faults by frequency. Gentilcore lists faults 'to name a few' and says only that many trainees reach the dumbbell to the floor (c7); StrengthLog's hip-rotation cue (c5) is not ranked either.

tells.text: Weight sits in the standing heel

plate.variantLine: Dumbbell drawn (one dumbbell, opposite hand, c1). Bodyweight version: every body-position claim (c2, c5, c6, c8, c10, c11, c12) holds; the grip and load claims (c3, c14, c18) apply to the dumbbell only.

grip.type: One dumbbell, held in the hand opposite the standing leg, arm hanging straight.
grip.width: One hand; the dumbbell lowers in front of the standing leg.
grip.handContact: Handle across the middle of the palm, gripped hard.

setup.step: Hold one dumbbell in the hand opposite your standing leg.
Stand on that leg with the knee soft, about 15-20 degrees.
Balance shaky? Keep the free leg's toes touching the floor.
Do all reps on one leg, then switch.

posture.point: Hips back; don't reach the dumbbell down.
Head to heel in one straight line, neck neutral.
Hips level; the lifted side does not turn up.
Weight back in the standing heel.
A shorter range is fine while control builds.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Reaching the dumbbell to the floor and rounding.
handlingMistakes.fix: Stop around mid-shin with a flat back.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Opening the hip of the lifted leg.
handlingMistakes.fix: Keep both hips pointing at the floor; shorten the range if needed.
Push the hips back and sit into the standing heel.

rows.where: Back of the standing thigh near the bottom
rows.means: Usually means the hips are hinging correctly.
Usually means the glutes are driving you back up.

rows.where: Lower back pain, or pain or numbness down both legs

risks.risk: One of the hardest single-leg movements; balance and form break easily.
Rounding the back while reaching low.

zooms.right: Head, back and free leg in one straight line.
zooms.wrong: Rounded back and shoulders, head craned up.

libraryDiff.why: Library primary hamstrings and secondary glutes match (c14). Add lower_back as secondary: Mo 2023 measured erector spinae activity that rose with opposite-side loading (c15).
